analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to prove age and other job discrimination in court.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a bipartisan group of four senators, never received a committee vote or a floor vote in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2009 Supreme Court decision made it much harder for older workers to win age discrimination cases: they had to prove age was the deciding reason they were fired or demoted, rather than one reason among several. This bill would reverse that for age discrimination and apply the same easier standard to claims based on race, sex, religion, national origin, and disability. It would let workers win with evidence that age or disability was simply a motivating factor, even if the employer had other reasons too — though if the employer proves it would have made the same decision anyway, the worker gets a ruling and lawyer's fees but no money damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers over 40 who face age discrimination in hiring, firing, or layoffs, and workers with disabilities and workers facing race, sex, religion, or national origin discrimination, all of whom would have an easier legal path to prove discrimination. Federal employees are covered too.

how_it_helps.text: Lets a worker prove discrimination by showing age or disability was a motivating factor, instead of the single decisive cause required after the Supreme Court's Gross v. FBL Financial decision.
Allows workers to rely on any type of admissible evidence, and rejects the requirement that they prove the protected characteristic was the sole cause of the employer's action.

Applies the same easier standard of proof to claims under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, so protection is consistent across discrimination laws.

Caps remedies in mixed-motive cases: a worker who shows discrimination was a motivating factor but cannot show the employer would have acted differently gets declaratory and injunctive relief and attorney's fees, but no money damages or reinstatement order — a limit meant to balance the easier standard with employer fairness.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face more lawsuits they find harder to defend, and would more often have to pay settlements, judgments, and attorney's fees when discrimination is shown to be one of the reasons for an employment decision.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to all claims pending on or after enactment, so employers would face the new, easier standard even in lawsuits already in progress.

An employer can avoid paying damages in a mixed-motive case only by proving it would have made the same decision without the discriminatory motive — a heavy burden that raises litigation costs and settlement values for employers even in close cases.

Defenders of the current 'but-for' standard argue it is a fairer causation bar: a worker whose employer had a legitimate, decisive reason should not be able to recover damages merely because age also played some role.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gain is real: after Gross v. FBL, age discrimination claims became very hard to win, and this bill would restore a standard Congress had already adopted for race and sex discrimination in 1991. The bill does moderate the cost to employers by capping remedies when the employer proves it would have acted the same way anyway. The main honest objection is the retroactive application to pending cases and higher litigation exposure for employers; the main honest concession on the other side is that discrimination is usually concealed, so requiring workers to prove one single decisive cause makes real discrimination nearly impossible to prove.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended, so no one ever voted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey introduced the bill on February 27, 2017, joined by Sens. Chuck Grassley, Patrick Leahy, and Susan Collins — two Democrats and two Republicans.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: they keep the harder-to-meet burden of proof from Gross v. FBL, making discrimination claims easier to defeat in court.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had an even bipartisan split at introduction — two Democratic and two Republican sponsors — but with only three additional cosponsors and no committee or floor vote ever scheduled, the record shows no party-line fight over it.

industries.note: The bill would make discrimination lawsuits easier to win by lowering the worker's burden of proof, raising employers' litigation and settlement costs. The interest in keeping the stricter Gross standard runs against older workers' ability to hold employers accountable.
More viable discrimination claims mean more cases and more attorney's-fee awards for lawyers representing workers; the bill's remedial cap keeps that gain moderate in mixed-motive cases.
